bib.title: Stochastic Processes and Markov Chains (Chapter 3 of Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: Bandit Algorithms, Cambridge University Press (book chapter)

question: What measure-theoretic machinery is needed to define infinite sequences of random variables, Markov chains, martingales and stopping times used later in the book?
contributions: Existence of infinite independent sequences and general stochastic processes (Thms 3.1, 3.2)
Markov kernels and Ionescu-Tulcea existence of Markov chains (Thm 3.3)
Martingales, stopping times, Doob optional stopping and maximal inequalities (Defs 3.4, 3.6, Thms 3.8-3.10)

results.claim: Doob's optional stopping: for a martingale and stopping time under any of three conditions, E[X_tau] = E[X_0]; super/submartingale gives an inequality.
results.setup: Theorem 3.8; needs bounded tau, or E[tau]<inf with bounded conditional increments, or bounded stopped process; discrete time, filtration F
results.quote: Then Xτ is almost surely well deﬁned, and E[Xτ] = E[X0].

results.claim: A clever stopping rule cannot make a fair gambler's expected winnings positive unless E[tau] is infinite.
results.setup: Gambler with Rademacher coin flips, S_t martingale; S_tau almost surely well defined

results.claim: Maximal inequality: a non-negative supermartingale exceeds epsilon at any time with probability at most E[X0]/epsilon (strengthens Markov's inequality).
results.setup: Supermartingale X_t >= 0 a.s., any epsilon>0, discrete time
results.quote:
Let (Xt)∞
t=0 be a supermartingale with
Xt ≥0 almost surely for all t.

results.claim: Maximal inequality for non-negative submartingales over a finite horizon.
results.setup: Submartingale X_t >= 0, horizon n, epsilon>0; proof left to Exercise 3.8
results.quote:
Let (Xt)n
t=0 be a submartingale with Xt ≥0 almost surely for
all t.

results.claim: Ionescu-Tulcea: an initial law and a sequence of kernels from the product of earlier spaces define a process whose finite-dimensional laws are the kernel products; any Markov chain with given kernel exists.
results.setup: Arbitrary measurable spaces, no Borel assumption
results.quote:
Then there exists a probability
space (Ω, F, P) and random elements (Xt)∞
t=1 with Xt : Ω→Ωt such that
PX1,...,Xn = Nn
t=1 Kt for all n ∈N+.

results.claim: Regular conditional distributions exist when X is Borel, giving the chain rule P_{X,Y} = P_Y (x) P_{X|Y}; this is the converse of Ionescu-Tulcea.
results.setup: X Borel; K unique up to a P_Y-null set
results.quote:
Then there exists a probability
kernel K from Y to X such that K(· | Y ) = P (X ∈· | Y ) P-almost surely.

limits: Pure measure-theoretic background: no algorithms, no bandit or RL results, no MDP content, no experiments.
Discrete time only; countable index set T=N; Markov chain theory (convergence, mixing) deferred to Chapters 37 and 38 for finite state spaces.
Theorem 3.1 proof is only a sketch; most proofs are left as exercises.
Authors expect most readers to skip it on first reading.
practices: Treat this chapter as reference: skip on first reading and consult it when infinite sequences of random variables arise (p.46)

Use Ionescu-Tulcea to justify that an interaction between a learner and an environment, defined by kernels, is a well-defined probability space (inferred from Thm 3.3 and its use for sequences of kernels)
Check the optional stopping conditions (a)-(c) before applying E[X_tau]=E[X_0]; the maximal inequality is the tool when they fail (p.51)

terms.definition: an inﬁnite sequence of random elements (Xt)∞ t=1 where the conditional distribution of Xt+1 given X1, . . . , Xt is the same as the conditional distribution of Xt+1 given Xt
a function K : X × G →[0, 1] such that K(x, ·) is a measure for all x and K(·, A) is F-measurable for all A
Markov chain whose kernel does not change with time; time-dependent kernels reduce to this by augmenting the state with a time component
F-adapted, integrable sequence with E[Xt | Ft-1] = Xt-1 almost surely; supermartingale uses less-than, submartingale greater-than
random variable tau in N U {inf} such that I{tau <= t} is Ft-measurable for all t
measures (mu_n) with mu_{n+1}(A x Omega_{n+1}) = mu_n(A)
a measurable space isomorphic to (A, B(A)) with A a Borel subset of the reals
